title: Erasmus
hook: a scholar prints the Greek New Testament and wants the ploughboy singing scripture

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gregorian chant: plainsong, one line of melody carrying the Psalms through the day. Your line was one line, sung.

Proof sheets, the ink still wet, spread across a table in a printer's shop in Basel. A priest leans over them, correcting as fast as they come. Each page has two columns. On one side, the New Testament in Greek, the language its writers used. On the other, a fresh Latin translation he has made himself. Readers who've known the gospels all their lives in one familiar Latin wording can now check it against the Greek, line by line. Some will be thrilled. Some will be furious.
screen: `GREEK ON ONE SIDE, LATIN ON THE OTHER.`

segments.voice: Desiderius Erasmus was a priest and scholar from Rotterdam who traveled widely, writing letters, editing old books, and poking fun at the church he loved. He belonged to a movement called humanism, and its rallying cry was two Latin words: ad fontes. To the springs. Back to the sources. Drink the water where it comes out of the rock, not after it has run down a long pipe. For Erasmus, the spring was the Greek of the New Testament, and the early Christian writers who read it. So he gathered Greek manuscripts, compared them, and printed a Greek text beside his own Latin. Where his Latin differed from the familiar wording, some readers were alarmed. His answer, roughly: loving the text means looking hard at it. In the preface, a little essay he called the Paraclesis, the exhortation, he says something that still sounds bold. He wishes the scriptures could be read by everyone, women too, and turned into every language. He pictures the farmer singing a piece of it behind the plough, the weaver humming it at the loom, the traveler shortening the road with its stories. Erasmus stayed in the Catholic church all his life. He wanted it cleaned up from the inside, by learning and by plain imitation of Christ, not torn apart. Soon others would take his Greek text and his questions much further than he ever meant to go. A saying went around that Erasmus laid the egg and Luther hatched it. Erasmus did not enjoy that one.

Take the angels' song from Luke: the King James Bible says, "on earth peace, good will toward men," and the Douay-Rheims, an old Catholic English translation, says, "on earth peace to men of good will." Say each slowly in your head, and notice where they meet and where they part, without deciding which is right, the way Erasmus set his two columns side by side. If you pray, rest on whichever line speaks to you.
Erasmus. A priest and scholar who printed the Greek New Testament beside his own Latin, wanted scripture in every language, and called people back to the sources.
Your line: back to the sources. A good question starts at the spring. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians in many churches study the Bible alongside its Greek and Hebrew, and comparing translations side by side is a common part of Bible study groups and sermon preparation.

chat.says: What did ad fontes mean for Erasmus?
options: Back to the sources: he went to the Greek New Testament and printed it beside his Latin.
Stay with the Latin: he wanted scholars to read only the wording the church already used.
Leave the church: he wanted readers to break away and start over on their own.
chat.meaning: Ad fontes means to the springs. Erasmus went back to the Greek of the New Testament, and stayed in the church, hoping to renew it from inside.

notes: Claims rule: the index date (1516) is not stated in the voice. The printer's location (Basel, Johann Froben's press), 'from Rotterdam', and that he stayed Catholic all his life are general history, not from the cited text; confirm.

Paraclesis paraphrase: the wish that women read the gospels, that scripture be translated into all languages, and the images of the farmer at the plough, the weaver at the loom, and the traveler. Confirm the paraphrase.
'Erasmus laid the egg and Luther hatched it' is given as 'a saying went around'; Erasmus's reported reply was that he laid a hen's egg and Luther hatched a different bird. Confirm attribution.

Practice compares Luke 2:14 in the KJV and Douay-Rheims without explaining the reason (a Greek textual variant); deliberately left unexplained under the claims rule. Confirm both quotations are exact.
Overlap check: day 833 (Wycliffe, 'the ploughman's bible') uses a ploughman image; this day keeps the plough to one sentence from the Paraclesis.
Editor pass: 'spent his life on the road' (overstated) changed to 'traveled widely'; otherwise checked and left as written.
Original left null: 'ad fontes' is taught in the teach and trapdoor instead.
Second editor: hook no longer opens on a thumping press (day 838 opened on Gutenberg's press); it opens on the proof sheets, and the invented portrait detail 'thin, sharp-eyed' is cut.

Auditor (day 847-856 pass): checked; Luke 2:14 matches KJV and Douay-Rheims (Challoner). The 1516 Latin was a revision of the Vulgate more than a wholly fresh translation (fuller in 1519); 'a fresh Latin translation he has made himself' is acceptable shorthand, confirm.
